Overview

This vignette illustrates deterministic calibration of Bayesian one-sample and paired tt-test designs for continuous clinical endpoints. The examples are prospective, trial-inspired design illustrations; they do not reproduce the original trials’ analyses or numerical results.

The function calibrate_bf_ttest() searches the requested range of sample sizes and returns the smallest feasible integer sample size. It evaluates evidence using the Bayes factor BF01BF_{01}, where smaller values favour H1H_1 and larger values favour H0H_0.

The package supports three hypotheses:

H0:δ=0versusH1:δ≠0, H_0:\delta=0 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_1:\delta\ne0,

H0:δ=0versusH1:δ>0, H_0:\delta=0 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_1:\delta>0,

and

H0:δ≤0versusH1:δ>0. H_0:\delta\le0 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_1:\delta>0.

Here, δ\delta is the standardized mean effect. For directional examples, the endpoint is coded so that positive values represent clinical benefit.

Example 1: Two-sided point-null design

This example is inspired by a phase-2 COPD study involving ivacaftor, compare Vijaykumar et al. (2025). We consider a hypothetical single-arm proof-of-concept study whose endpoint is change in prebronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) percent predicted at Day 84.

Suppose that a 5-percentage-point improvement is clinically relevant and that the planning standard deviation is 12.5 percentage points. The corresponding standardized effect is

δA=512.5=0.40. \delta_A = \frac{5}{12.5} = 0.40.

We use the two-sided point-null hypothesis

H0:δ=0versusH1:δ≠0. H_0:\delta=0 \quad\text{versus}\quad H_1:\delta\ne0.

The analysis prior under H1H_1 is N(0,0.52)N(0, 0.5^2). This prior defines the Bayes factor used at analysis; it is not the same as the design prior used to evaluate operating characteristics.

The design prior under H0H_0 is a point mass at δ=0\delta=0. Under H1H_1, we use a truncated normal design prior centred at the anticipated beneficial effect, TN(0.40,0.202;[0,∞))TN(0.40, 0.20^2; [0,\infty)). This represents uncertainty about the size of a beneficial effect while excluding harmful effects from the beneficial-effect planning scenario.

pulmonary_normal_dp <- calibrate_bf_ttest(
  design = "one.sample",
  hypothesis = "two.sided.pointnull",

  # Search range for the number of evaluable participants
  n_min = 20,
  n_max = 200,

  # Evidence thresholds:
  # BF01 <= 0.10 is compelling evidence for H1;
  # BF01 >= 3 is compelling evidence for H0.
  k1 = 1 / 10,
  k0 = 3,

  # Analysis prior under H1: N(0, 0.5^2)
  analysis_prior_sd = 0.5,

  # Error probability for incorrectly obtaining evidence for H1
  # when the true standardized effect is exactly zero.
  freq_t1e = 0.05,
  bayes_t1e = 0.05,

  # Frequentist power at the clinically relevant point alternative.
  freq_power = list(
    main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)
  ),

  # Average probability of evidence for H1 under the H1 design prior.
  bayes_power = 0.80,

  # Probability of compelling evidence for H0 under the H0 design prior.
  # Including this argument also computes and stores the H0 evidence region.
  pce_h0 = 0.60,

  # Design priors used only for operating-characteristic calculations.
  design_prior_h0 = list(type = "point", effect = 0),
  design_prior_h1 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = 0.40,
    sd = 0.20,
    lower = 0,
    upper = Inf
  ),

  control = control_full_fast
)

print(pulmonary_normal_dp)

The printed result reports the selected sample size n*n^*, the decision regions on the observed-tt scale, and the attained values of every active constraint. For this configuration, the calibrated result is n*=161n^*=161 (df=160df=160); the evidence-for-H1H_1 region is approximately t≤−2.95t\le -2.95 or t≥2.95t\ge 2.95.

plot(pulmonary_normal_dp)

Figure 1: Output of the plot function for a one-sample Bayesian two-sided point-null t-test design based on full calibration. Both Bayesian and frequentist power and type-I-error are calibrated jointly.

The frequentist type-I error is the probability, at δ=0\delta=0, of obtaining BF01≤0.10BF_{01}\le 0.10, that is, compelling evidence for H1H_1 when the point null is true. The Bayesian type-I error averages that same probability over the H0H_0 design prior. Because the H0H_0 design prior here is a point mass at zero, these two values coincide.

The operating-characteristic plot displays their shared curve as “Frequentist type-I error” rather than drawing two coincident curves and repeating the legend entry.

The frequentist power constraint evaluates Pδ=0.40(BF01≤0.10)P_{\delta=0.40}(BF_{01}\le 0.10). In contrast, bayes_power averages Pδ(BF01≤0.10)P_{\delta}(BF_{01}\le 0.10) over the continuous H1H_1 design prior. Thus, the two power requirements answer different planning questions.

The pce_h0 constraint evaluates the probability of obtaining compelling evidence for the null, BF01≥3BF_{01}\ge3, under the H0H_0 design prior. This implies that a minimum probability of obtaining a Bayes factor in favour of H0H_0 of at least size 33 or larger is fixed, when H0H_0 is true. In this example, it also causes the function to calculate the central evidence-for-H0H_0 region. The interval is shown by the printed object and by the blue-shaded region in the decision-function plot in the top left.

The decision panel displays log⁡(BF01)\log(BF_{01}). The orange dashed line denotes log⁡(k1)\log(k_1), so values below it support H1H_1; the blue dashed line denotes log⁡(k0)\log(k_0), so values above it support H0H_0. The shaded regions represent the stored decision regions: orange for evidence for H1H_1, blue for evidence for H0H_0, and grey for inconclusive results. The sample-size panel shows the operating characteristics throughout the search and marks the selected n*n^*.

A brief comparison of calibration modes

The first example above calibrated both frequentist and Bayesian operating characteristics such as power and type-I-error jointly. Also, the probability of compelling evidence for H0H_0 was calibrated. Next, we compare the different calibration modes available. We can pick whatever combination we like as the calibration target, but the most prominent choices might include:

  • Frequentist calibration
  • Bayesian calibration
  • Hybrid calibration
  • Full calibration

We use identical arguments including our design and analysis priors for all calibrations below, as specified in the following code chunk:

library(bfbin2arm)

vignette_control <- resolve_control_bf_ttest()

common_args <- list(
  design = "one.sample",
  hypothesis = "two.sided.pointnull",

  n_min = 20,
  n_max = 200,

  # BF01 <= 0.10: evidence for H1
  # BF01 >= 3: available as a reference threshold, but no PCE constraint here
  k1 = 1 / 10,
  k0 = 3,

  # Analysis prior under H1: N(0, 0.5^2)
  analysis_prior_sd = 0.5,

  # H0 design prior: exact null
  design_prior_h0 = list(type = "point", effect = 0),

  # H1 design prior: uncertain beneficial effect
  design_prior_h1 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = 0.40,
    sd = 0.20,
    lower = 0,
    upper = Inf
  ),

  control = control_full_fast
)

Frequentist calibration

This design requires frequentist type-I error at most 0.05 and frequentist power at δ=0.40\delta=0.40 of at least 0.80.

pulmonary_freq <- do.call(
  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    common_args,
    list(
      freq_t1e = 0.05,
      freq_power = list(
        main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)
      )
    )
  )
)

print(pulmonary_freq)

Bayesian calibration

This design requires Bayesian type-I error at most 0.05 and Bayesian power of at least 0.80 under the specified H1H_1 design prior.

pulmonary_bayes <- do.call(
  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    common_args,
    list(
      bayes_t1e = 0.05,
      bayes_power = 0.80
    )
  )
)

print(pulmonary_bayes)

Hybrid calibration

This hybrid design controls type-I error at the exact null and requires average Bayesian power under the H1 design prior.

pulmonary_bayes_power_freq_t1e <- do.call(
  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    common_args,
    list(
      freq_t1e = 0.05,
      bayes_power = 0.80
    )
  )
)

Full calibration

This activates all four error/power constraints, but deliberately does not require a minimum probability of compelling evidence for H0H_0.

pulmonary_full_no_pce <- do.call(
  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    common_args,
    list(
      freq_t1e = 0.05,
      bayes_t1e = 0.05,
      freq_power = list(
        main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)
      ),
      bayes_power = 0.80

      # Deliberately omit:
      # pce_h0 = ...
    )
  )
)

print(pulmonary_full_no_pce)

The frequentist-only calibration selects n*=88n^*=88, because it requires 80% probability of evidence for H1H_1 only at the single planning effect δ=0.40\delta=0.40. The Bayesian-power requirement averages this probability over the H1 design prior, which includes smaller positive effects; this produces the larger sample size n*=161n^*=161.

The Bayesian-only, Bayesian-power-plus-frequentist-type-I-error, and full no-PCE calibrations select the same sample size in this illustration. This occurs because the H0H_0 design prior is a point mass at δ=0\delta=0, making the Bayesian and frequentist type-I error quantities numerically identical, and because the attained frequentist power at δ=0.40\delta=0.40 already exceeds its 0.80 target at n=161n=161. No calibration includes a PCE requirement. Hence, none requires a minimum probability of compelling evidence for H0H_0.

Example 2: Directional point-null design

Consider the same pulmonary endpoint when the confirmatory scientific question is restricted to benefit. The directional point-null test compares H0:δ=0H_0:\delta=0 with H1:δ>0H_1:\delta>0.

The analysis prior under H1H_1 is a normal distribution truncated to positive standardized effects, N(0,0.52)𝕀(δ>0)N(0, 0.5^2)\mathbb{I}(\delta>0). Consequently, an adverse observed change does not provide evidence for the beneficial alternative. The design prior under H1H_1 represents uncertainty about the anticipated beneficial effect.

directional_common_args <- list(
  design = "one.sample",
  hypothesis = "greater.pointnull",

  # Search range for the number of evaluable participants.
  n_min = 20,
  n_max = 200,

  # BF01 <= 0.10: compelling evidence for benefit (H1).
  # BF01 >= 3: available as a decision threshold, but no PCE constraint is
  # imposed in the calibrations below.
  k1 = 1 / 10,
  k0 = 3,

  # Directional H1 analysis prior:
  # N(0, 0.5^2), truncated to delta > 0.
  analysis_prior_sd = 0.5,

  # H0 design prior: exact null effect.
  design_prior_h0 = list(type = "point", effect = 0),

  # H1 design prior: uncertain beneficial effect.
  design_prior_h1 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = 0.40,
    sd = 0.20,
    lower = 0,
    upper = Inf
  ),

  control = control_full_fast
)

Frequentist calibration

This design controls frequentist type-I error at the exact null and requires frequentist power of at least 80% at δ=0.40\delta=0.40.

pulmonary_directional_freq <- do.call(
  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    directional_common_args,
    list(
      freq_t1e = 0.05,
      freq_power = list(
        main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)
      )
    )
  )
)

print(pulmonary_directional_freq)

We see that the number of patients decreases compared to the two-sided test. We can plot the design:

plot(pulmonary_directional_freq)

Figure 2: Output of the plot function for a one-sample Bayesian t-test design based on frequentist calibration.

Figure 2 shows that the shape of the decision function now reflects the one-sided test. For increasingly large t-statistic, the Bayes factor will reject H0H_0. Note that the top right panel in Figure 2 shows Bayesian power (as the design prior under H1H_1 is specified in the common parameters above), but only frequentist power and type-I-error are used for calibrating the required sample size.

Bayesian calibration

This design controls the H0H_0-design-prior average probability of incorrectly obtaining compelling evidence for benefit and requires 80% average Bayesian power under the H1H_1 design prior.

pulmonary_directional_bayes <- do.call(
  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    directional_common_args,
    list(
      bayes_t1e = 0.05,
      bayes_power = 0.80
    )
  )
)

print(pulmonary_directional_bayes)

Since the Bayesian type-I-error under H0:δ=0H_0:\delta = 0 is computed under a point-prior, the Bayesian type-I-error rate is identical to the frequentist one. This is the reason that the plot shows frequentist type-I-error (which usually is more conservative), even though the calibration uses Bayesian type-I-error (and power).

plot(pulmonary_directional_bayes)

Figure 3: Output of the plot function for a one-sample Bayesian t-test design based on Bayesian calibration.

This hybrid calibration uses a frequentist type-I error requirement at δ=0\delta=0 and a Bayesian power requirement averaged over the H1H_1 design prior.

  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    directional_common_args,
    list(
      freq_t1e = 0.05,
      bayes_power = 0.80
    )
  )
)

Full calibration without PCE

This version activates frequentist and Bayesian type-I error requirements, as well as frequentist and Bayesian power requirements. It does not impose a probability-of-compelling-evidence (PCE) requirement for H0H_0.

pulmonary_directional_full_no_pce <- do.call(
  calibrate_bf_ttest,
  c(
    directional_common_args,
    list(
      freq_t1e = 0.05,
      bayes_t1e = 0.05,
      freq_power = list(
        main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)
      ),
      bayes_power = 0.80
    )
  )
)

print(pulmonary_directional_full_no_pce)

   P_delta=0(BF01 <= k1) 0.00431281   0.05

 P_design,H1(BF01 <= k1) 0.80025788   0.80
 P_delta=0.4(BF01 <= k1) 0.97401497   0.80

        <= 0.0456871901      TRUE
        <= 0.0456871901      TRUE
        >= 0.0002578833      TRUE
        >= 0.1740149710      TRUE

We see that all calibrations except the frequentit one require n⋆=134n^{\star}=134 patients. Frequentist calibration under the much more optimistic point prior at δ=0.4\delta = 0.4 requires solely n⋆=75n^{\star}=75 patients.

The point-null versus greater directional test shows that the directional Bayes factor is asymmetric in the observed tt statistic, compare the top left panel in Figure 2. The region providing evidence for H1H_1 should therefore occur in the positive tail only. The implementation determines decision regions by finding the relevant Bayes-factor roots and classifying the resulting intervals rather than imposing a symmetric decision geometry.

Example 3: Directional composite-null design

This example is inspired by an 8-week open-label, multicentre study of inhaled tobramycin in people with cystic fibrosis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, compare Sutharsan et al. (2020). The published study assessed pulmonary outcomes including forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and lung-clearance index (LCI).

We consider a hypothetical future single-arm proof-of-concept study. Let the endpoint be improvement in LCI from baseline to Week 8, coded as baseline minus follow-up LCI. Thus, a positive value denotes clinical improvement.

The scientific question is whether the intervention provides evidence of benefit rather than merely evidence against an exact zero mean change:

H0:δ≤0versusH1:δ>0. H_0:\delta\leq0 \quad\text{versus}\quad H_1:\delta>0.

The null-side hypothesis includes both no improvement and deterioration. This is appropriate when a benefit claim should be made only when the study yields compelling evidence for an improvement.

composite_lci_continuous <- calibrate_bf_ttest(
  design = "one.sample",
  hypothesis = "greater.composite",
  n_min = 20,
  n_max = 120,
  k1 = 1 / 20,
  k0 = 3,

  analysis_prior_h0 = make_analysis_prior_less_equal(sd = 0.5),
  analysis_prior_h1 = make_analysis_prior_greater(sd = 0.5),

  freq_t1e = 0.05,
  freq_power = list(main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)),
  bayes_t1e = 0.05,
  bayes_power = 0.80,
  pce_h0 = 0.60,

  design_prior_h0 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = -0.10,
    sd = 0.25,
    lower = -Inf,
    upper = 0
  ),
  design_prior_h1 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = 0.40,
    sd = 0.20,
    lower = 0,
    upper = Inf
  ),

  control = fast_control
)

composite_lci_continuous

Figure 3: Output of the plot function for a one-sample Bayesian composite-null versus directional t-test design based on full calibration. Both Bayesian and frequentist power and type-I-error are calibrated jointly. Also, a 60% threshold on the probability of compelling evidence for the null hypothesis is guaranteed.

As a sidenote, single-arm change-from-baseline evidence is vulnerable to within-person variability, natural history, regression to the mean, and measurement error; it does not itself establish a causal treatment effect, in contrast to two-arm change-from-baseline evidence. However, the composite-null formulation clarifies the evidential decision rule. What it cannot achieve, however, it to remove the limitations of a non-comparative design. External controls, randomization, or other design features may be necessary for a confirmatory efficacy claim. We study this example nevertheless, because a directional composite-null design is widely used in clinical trials.

Comparison with a conventional frequentist design

The conventional comparator is a one-sided one-sample t-test,

H0:δ≤0versusH1:δ>0, H_0: \delta \leq 0 \qquad \text{versus} \qquad H_1: \delta > 0,

designed for a type-I error rate of 0.05 and 80% power at the fixed alternative δ=0.40\delta = 0.40. We also consider a Bayes-factor design that retains the frequentist type-I-error and power requirements but does not require compelling evidence for the H0 region. This separates the sample-size implication of requiring strong evidence for H1 from the additional requirement to obtain compelling H0 evidence.

## Conventional frequentist one-sided one-sample t-test
freq_design <- power.t.test(
  delta = 0.40,
  sd = 1,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = "one.sample",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)

freq_n <- ceiling(freq_design$n)
## Bayes-factor design: H1 evidence only, no PCE requirement.
composite_lci_no_pce <- calibrate_bf_ttest(
  design = "one.sample",
  hypothesis = "greater.composite",
  n_min = 20,
  n_max = 120,
  k1 = 1 / 20,
  k0 = 3,

  analysis_prior_h0 = make_analysis_prior_less_equal(sd = 0.5),
  analysis_prior_h1 = make_analysis_prior_greater(sd = 0.5),

  freq_t1e = 0.05,
  freq_power = list(main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)),

  design_prior_h0 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = -0.10,
    sd = 0.25,
    lower = -Inf,
    upper = 0
  ),
  design_prior_h1 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = 0.40,
    sd = 0.20,
    lower = 0,
    upper = Inf
  ),

  control = fast_control
)
sample_size_comparison <- data.frame(
  design = c(
    "Frequentist one-sample t-test",
    "Bayes-factor design: H1 evidence only",
    "Bayes-factor design: H1 and H0 evidence"
  ),
  type_I_error_control = c(
    "One-sided alpha = 0.05",
    "P(delta = 0; BF01 <= 1/20) <= 0.05",
    "P(delta = 0; BF01 <= 1/20) <= 0.05"
  ),
  power_requirement = c(
    "Power(delta = 0.40) >= 0.80",
    "P(delta = 0.40; BF01 <= 1/20) >= 0.80",
    "P(delta = 0.40; BF01 <= 1/20) >= 0.80"
  ),
  H0_evidence_requirement = c(
    "None",
    "None",
    "P_design,H0(BF01 >= 3) >= 0.60"
  ),
  sample_size = c(
    freq_n,
    composite_lci_no_pce$n,
    composite_lci_continuous$n
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

The conventional frequentist calculation requires 41 patients. The BF design without a probability-of-compelling-evidence (PCE) requirement requires 43 patients. Its slightly larger sample size reflects the use of the more stringent evidential criterion BF01≤1/20BF_{01} \leq 1/20, rather than a conventional one-sided significance threshold.

Adding the requirement that the design yield compelling H0H_0 evidence (BF01≥3BF_{01} \geq 3) with probability at least 0.60 under the H0H_0 design prior increases the required sample size to 65. Thus, the PCE requirement adds 22 patients beyond the H1H_1-evidence-only BF design, and the complete calibrated design adds 24 patients beyond the conventional frequentist design.

Example 4: Paired one-sample design

This example is inspired by the Healthy BP study, which compared a dietitian-led telehealth lifestyle intervention with a self-directed intervention. Its primary endpoint was change in 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure from baseline to 12 weeks, see Taher et al. (2021).

Here, we consider a hypothetical future single-group implementation study with measurements at the same two time points. This is a prospective design illustration, not a reproduction of the original randomized trial or its between-group analysis. All effect sizes, prior distributions, evidence thresholds, and calibration targets below are illustrative planning assumptions rather than quantities attributed to that trial.

Paired outcome and hypothesis

Define the participant-level outcome as

Di=Xi,baseline−Xi,12weeks, D_i = X_{i,\mathrm{baseline}} - X_{i,\mathrm{12\ weeks}},

so that a positive difference represents a beneficial reduction in systolic blood pressure. Let

μD=𝔼(Di),σD=SD⁡(Di),δ=μDσD. \mu_D = \mathbb{E}(D_i), \qquad \sigma_D = \operatorname{SD}(D_i), \qquad \delta = \frac{\mu_D}{\sigma_D}.

A clinically relevant reduction of 5 mmHg and an assumed planning standard deviation of paired differences of 12.5 mmHg imply

δA=512.5=0.40. \delta_A = \frac{5}{12.5} = 0.40.

The standard deviation in this calculation is the standard deviation of the within-participant differences, not the standard deviation of baseline or follow-up blood pressure considered separately.

We use the directional composite-null hypotheses

H0:δ≤0versusH1:δ>0. H_0:\delta\leq0 \qquad\text{versus}\qquad H_1:\delta>0.

Thus, the null-side hypothesis includes both no mean reduction and a mean increase in blood pressure.

For a paired design, nn is the number of participants with evaluable baseline and follow-up measurements. The test statistic is

T=nD‾SD,T∣δ∼tn−1(nδ). T = \frac{\sqrt{n}\,\bar D}{S_D}, \qquad T\mid\delta \sim t_{n-1}(\sqrt{n}\delta).

The statistical engine is therefore the same as for a one-sample test of the participant-level differences.

Priors, evidence thresholds, and calibration targets

We use normal analysis priors with scale 0.5, truncated and normalized on the respective hypothesis regions:

δ∣H0∼N(0,0.52)|(−∞,0],δ∣H1∼N(0,0.52)|(0,∞). \delta\mid H_0 \sim N(0,0.5^2)\big|_{(-\infty,0]}, \qquad \delta\mid H_1 \sim N(0,0.5^2)\big|_{(0,\infty)}.

These analysis priors define the Bayes factor. For planning, we use separate design priors:

πd,0=N(−0.10,0.252)|(−∞,0],πd,1=N(0.40,0.202)|(0,∞). \pi_{d,0} = N(-0.10,0.25^2)\big|_{(-\infty,0]}, \qquad \pi_{d,1} = N(0.40,0.20^2)\big|_{(0,\infty)}.

The evidence thresholds are fixed in advance:

  • BF01≤1/20BF_{01}\leq1/20: compelling evidence for a beneficial reduction;
  • BF01≥3BF_{01}\geq3: compelling evidence for the null-side hypothesis;
  • otherwise: an inconclusive result.

We jointly require:

  • pointwise frequentist type-I error at δ=0\delta=0 at most 0.05;
  • frequentist power at δ=0.40\delta=0.40 at least 0.80;
  • Bayesian type-I error under the null-side design prior at most 0.05;
  • Bayesian power under the beneficial-effect design prior at least 0.80;
  • probability of compelling null-side evidence under the null-side design prior at least 0.60.
paired_bp <- calibrate_bf_ttest(
  design = "paired",
  hypothesis = "greater.composite",

  # Number of evaluable participant pairs.
  n_min = 20,
  n_max = 120,

  # Prespecified, fixed evidence thresholds.
  k1 = 1 / 20,
  k0 = 3,

  # Default composite-null analysis priors:
  # N(0, 0.5^2), truncated to the respective half-lines.
  analysis_prior_sd = 0.5,

  freq_t1e = 0.05,
  freq_power = list(
    main = list(effect = 0.40, target = 0.80)
  ),
  bayes_t1e = 0.05,
  bayes_power = 0.80,
  pce_h0 = 0.60,

  design_prior_h0 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = -0.10,
    sd = 0.25,
    lower = -Inf,
    upper = 0
  ),
  design_prior_h1 = list(
    type = "truncnormal",
    mean = 0.40,
    sd = 0.20,
    lower = 0,
    upper = Inf
  ),

  control = control_full_fast
)

print(paired_bp)

Calibrated design

The selected sample size is n⋆=65n^\star = 65 evaluable participant pairs, with 6464 degrees of freedom. Thus, the design requires at least 6565 participants contributing both measurements, not 2⋅65=1302\cdot 65=130 independently sampled participants.

Interpretation and relation to the one-sample example

This example uses the same standardized-effect priors, fixed evidence thresholds, and calibration requirements as the composite-null one-sample example. Consequently, with identical numerical controls, the paired and one-sample calculations represent the same mathematical calibration problem. What changes is the interpretation of the outcome and sample size: here the observations are participant-level differences and nn counts evaluable pairs.

Repeated baseline and follow-up measurements are not independent observations. Their dependence is incorporated through the standard deviation of the paired differences. If planning information is available only for the marginal standard deviations and within-participant correlation, then

σD2=σbaseline2+σfollow-up2−2ρσbaselineσfollow-up. \sigma_D^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{follow\text{-}up}}^2 - 2\rho\, \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}} \sigma_{\mathrm{follow\text{-}up}}.

The assumed value σD=12.5\sigma_D=12.5 mmHg should therefore be justified using relevant paired data or examined in sensitivity analyses.

Finally, the calibrated sample size refers to evaluable pairs. Recruitment inflation for missing follow-up measurements should be considered separately. Neither such inflation nor the paired analysis itself resolves bias arising from informative missingness or the causal limitations of a single-group study.

Interpretation

calibrate_bf_ttest() returns the smallest sample size in the requested range that satisfies the activated constraints. The returned object includes the Bayes-factor evidence regions, attained operating characteristics, constraint table, and numerical controls used for the calculation.

The examples are illustrations of a design procedure. They do not imply that a Bayesian design automatically requires fewer participants than a conventional design; any difference follows from the chosen evidence thresholds and jointly calibrated operating-characteristic requirements.

Taher, Mohamed, Christina Yule, Heather Bonaparte, et al. 2021. “Telehealth Versus Self-Directed Lifestyle Intervention to Promote Healthy Blood Pressure: A Protocol for a Randomised Controlled Trial.” BMJ Open 11 (3): e044292. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2020-044292.
Vijaykumar, Kadambari, George M. Solomon, Jennifer Guimbellot, et al. 2025. “Ivacaftor for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: Results from a Phase 2, Randomized Controlled Trial.” Am J Respir Crit Care Med 211 (5): 823–31. https://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.202407-1302OC.
